operation_details.item: The user prefers blunt, directive wording with minimal softening when giving graduate students feedback on draft chapters.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: How is the dissertation chapter review going today?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I’m reviewing two draft chapters before our lab meeting. I prefer to give graduate students blunt, directive feedback with minimal softening.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: So you focus on clear action items rather than cushioning every criticism?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Exactly. I’ll write things like, “Rewrite this section around the central claim,” or “Remove the unsupported literature review.”

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That sounds efficient, especially with publication deadlines and grant work competing for your time.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: It is. The feedback should tell the student precisely what to change, not bury the recommendation under encouragement.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Would you use the same style when commenting on conference papers or lecture materials?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Usually, yes. I adjust the level of detail, but I keep the wording direct and revision-focused.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Completely forget my preference that When I give graduate students feedback on draft chapters, I want blunt, directive wording with minimal softening—for example, 'This section is inadequate' rather than 'You might consider strengthening this area'.
